title: Classifieds, Leads, Transactions and Managed Models: A Marketplace Taxonomy
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (one spec paragraph per draft unit, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, the three acceptance criteria, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the chapter's entry in journal-spec.json; the supporting claims T1 to T5 are written here.

know: The four rungs of the endpoint ladder (classifieds, lead generation, transactional, managed) and the six axes of a marketplace profile.
What each rung adds to identity, contexts, trust, ranking signal, monetization, data and regulation, and the documented moves along the ladder in both directions.
believe: The marketplace model is an architecture decision, not a pricing decision, and it belongs to a country and category, not to a brand.
can_do: Write a marketplace profile register for their own group and scope a move toward the transaction by category, with an exit plan.

audience.who: Experienced architects and engineering leaders working on listing marketplaces: chief and enterprise architects of marketplace groups, principal and staff engineers, search, data and ML leads, platform-engineering leads, product and engineering directors of classifieds, real-estate, automotive, jobs and recommerce marketplaces, and technology leaders integrating acquired marketplaces.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are.
How to make and defend an architecture decision.
does_not_know: Marketplace economics: liquidity, network effects, multi-homing.
Search and ML vocabulary: learning to rank, percolation, hybrid retrieval.
Regulatory detail: DSA statements of reasons, DAC7, P2B.
Vertical specifics: VINs, property and vehicle feed standards.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to add payments to a whole brand, the reader names what the move adds to the systems and how to scope it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A horizontal brand wants to add payments and buyer protection to its whole site, cars and homes included. Using only this chapter: what does the move add to the systems, and how should it be scoped?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It adds order, payment and buyer-protection contexts through a licensed payment partner, deeper seller identity and reporting such as DAC7, and changes what ranking and experiments can observe. Scope it per category (goods, not cars or homes, as leboncoin, Kleinanzeigen and Marktplaats did), record it as configuration in the profile register, and plan an exit, because OLX and others pulled back.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's twenty-row grid; the four models of the endpoint ladder; six axes and the marketplace profile; vertical differences; what each model asks of the architecture; documented moves along the ladder; Veldmark's profile register; where the marketplace should end; failure modes; the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: dated public company records and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: What kind of marketplace is this, and why does the answer decide the architecture?
thesis.claim: A listing marketplace is defined less by what it lists than by where its job ends (at the contact, a qualified lead, a completed payment and delivery, or a guaranteed outcome), and each step down that ladder adds bounded contexts, data, identity checks, liabilities and regulators; because one brand holds several models across countries and categories, and marketplaces move along the ladder in both directions, the endpoint must be recorded per country and category as configuration, and every move toward the transaction treated as a category-gated bet with an exit plan.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the business model is a pricing and product choice layered on one marketplace platform, that each brand has one model, and that the industry is heading to transactions everywhere, so every brand should be built for payments now.
thesis.so_what: An architect who accepts this keeps a versioned marketplace profile register that is reviewed whenever a brand proposes a model change, shares the capabilities beneath the endpoint first, and sizes a shared order and payment platform by the profiles that need it (three of Veldmark's twenty) rather than by brand.
thesis.how_why: A classifieds platform never sees the money, so it cannot observe whether a sale happened, and its ranking and experiments optimize contacts. Adding payment switches on licensed payment partners, seller reporting and buyer-protection risk, and the managed rung changes what a model error costs, as Zillow Offers' $304.4 million write-down showed. leboncoin, Kleinanzeigen and Marktplaats added payments for goods but not for cars or homes, and OLX de-prioritized pay-and-ship in Europe.

supporting_claims.claim: One brand holds several marketplace models across countries and categories, so the question of what kind of marketplace it is has to be answered per country and category, not per brand.

Marketplaces are classified first by endpoint, where the platform's job ends (at the contact, a qualified lead, a completed payment and delivery, or a guaranteed outcome), and five further axes complete a marketplace profile.
Each step down the endpoint ladder adds bounded contexts, data, identity checks, liabilities and regulators, and changes what the platform can observe and therefore optimize.
Marketplaces move along the ladder in both directions: moves toward the transaction have worked category by category, and several pushes have been scaled back or reversed.

The endpoint should therefore be recorded per country and category as configuration in a reviewed profile register, and each move toward the transaction treated as a category-gated bet with an exit plan.

role.contribution: Defines the marketplace models and the marketplace profile that the liquidity chapter measures and the capability and context chapters map.

additional_patterns.applies_to: the trade-offs, failure modes and Chief Architect sections, which turn the vocabulary and the record into recommendations

flow.rationale: Each section supplies what the next needs. The Veldmark grid poses the question before any term is defined; the four models define the endpoint; the six axes complete the profile; the vertical table reads the profile per vertical straight after its axes are defined; the consequences then take the axis that reaches furthest, the endpoint, into the systems; the documented moves need the consequences to show why moving is costly; Veldmark's register applies both. The three judgement sections (trade-offs, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view) then run together: the two judgements, what happens without them, and the standing decisions that keep them; the questions close the body. Defining the profile after the documented moves would leave the reader without the unit those moves are made in; four of the six draft-check readers (rounds 1 and 3) placed the vertical table directly after Six Axes.

hook.content: Ask five people in a marketplace group what kind of business it runs and you get five partly right answers: 'classifieds' (general manager), 'we are becoming transactional' (product director), 'we sell dealer subscriptions' (sales director), 'most of our money is advertising and visibility' (finance), 'a messaging platform with listings attached' (trust and safety lead).

bridge.from_reader_world: Each of the five answers describes a different point at which the marketplace's job ends.
bridge.to_topic: Each endpoint implies a different architecture, so the model is an architecture decision, not a pricing decision.

thesis_statement.text: The model is an architecture decision, not a pricing decision: moving the endpoint by one step adds bounded contexts, data, identity requirements, regulators and failure modes, so the decision must be explicit, recorded per country and category, and revisable, because marketplaces move in both directions.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout and paragraph p02.

roadmap.placement: Paragraph p03, which groups the chapter's sections into three steps (vocabulary, consequences, judgement) and names the later chapters that build on the marketplace profile.

promises.promise: Start with Veldmark's grid of twenty rows.
Define the four models of the endpoint ladder.
Add five more axes to make a marketplace profile.
Compare the typical profile of each vertical.
Show what each model asks of the systems.
Follow documented moves along the ladder in both directions, and Veldmark's register of profiles.
Weigh where a marketplace should end.
Show how the taxonomy fails, the Chief Architect's standing decisions and questions to ask.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Asked what kind of business their marketplace group runs, five people give five partly right answers, each describing a different end point of the marketplace's job and each implying a different architecture.

evidence.what: The general manager says 'classifieds', the product director 'we are becoming transactional', the sales director 'we sell dealer subscriptions', finance 'advertising and visibility', the trust and safety lead 'a messaging platform with listings attached'.
evidence.shows: One business seen from five seats yields five endpoints, which is the confusion the chapter's vocabulary resolves.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The model is an architecture decision, not a pricing decision: moving the endpoint by one step adds contexts, data, identity requirements, regulators and failure modes, so the decision must be explicit, recorded per country and category, and revisable.

transition_in.carries_over: Each answer implies a different architecture.
transition_in.introduces: The chapter's claim: the model is an architecture decision, recorded per country and category.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter gives the conversation a shared vocabulary in three stated steps: the vocabulary (an opening scene at Veldmark with its grid of twenty country-and-category rows, the four models, the six axes and the profile, the typical profile of each vertical), the consequences (what each model asks of the systems, documented moves along the ladder, Veldmark's register) and the judgement (where to end, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions); the marketplace profile it introduces is used by later chapters.

evidence.what: The sections in order; the terms the chapter owns; the later chapters that use the profile (liquidity-and-network-effects, business-capabilities, bounded-contexts, multi-country-platforms) and the neighbours that own history and vertical detail.
evidence.shows: Lets a reader of the opening predict the chapter and see where it sits in Part I.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that the model is an architecture decision.
transition_in.introduces: How the chapter builds the vocabulary to make that decision, section by section.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: One Group, Four Models
sections.controlling_idea: A proposal for one checkout across Veldmark's four brands assumed one marketplace model, and a grid of five questions showed the group ran at least four, spread over twenty rows that do not line up with brands.

advances_thesis.how: Shows on a concrete group that the model varies below the brand, which is why it must be recorded per country and category.

transition_in.introduces: Its first item: the Veldmark situation that poses the question.

flow.rationale: Proposal, grid, rows, the hardest row, then the conclusion: the order in which the afternoon happened, so the conclusion arrives with its evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's Group Chief Product Officer proposes extending Tradeyard Safe Deal into one listing and order platform for all four brands, on the strength of its 2026 results.

evidence.what: Common Ground: €140M over four years, approved January 2027; Safe Deal 2026: 11.6 million transactions, about €1.02 billion GMV, about €75 million revenue, a take rate of about 7%.
evidence.shows: The proposal rests on one brand's transactional success, which is the assumption the chapter tests.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ingrid answers the slide with a grid: brands and countries down the side, five questions about endpoint, supply, item identity, who holds the money and who loses first across the top.

evidence.what: The five questions on the grid.
evidence.shows: They are the axes the chapter later defines, asked in plain words.

transition_in.introduces: Ingrid's response: not an argument but a grid of questions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The grid had twenty rows whose answers did not line up with the brands: endpoints differed by country and category inside one brand, and Keybridge was not a marketplace at all.

evidence.what: Tradeyard goods ending at contact or at Safe Deal payment; Portugal without Safe Deal; Polish insertion-fee sections; Motorvane leads to 21,400 dealers; Hearthly leads and Valuo seller leads; Keybridge as SaaS.
evidence.shows: The model belongs to a country and category, not to a brand.

transition_in.introduces: What it showed by the end of the afternoon.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The most uncomfortable row was Poland, where Tradeyard's cars section and Motorvane served the same dealers under two different models.

evidence.what: Per-listing insertion fees on Tradeyard Poland against dealer subscriptions with slots on Motorvane Poland; both sales teams calling on the same showrooms.
evidence.shows: Two models in one market for one customer group are a commercial conflict that the architecture has to represent.

transition_in.introduces: The one row that showed a conflict, not only a difference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ingrid concluded that 'one checkout for four brands' assumed one model while the group ran at least four, and the rest of the chapter is the vocabulary she used to say why.

transition_in.carries_over: The grid and the Polish row.
transition_in.introduces: Ingrid's conclusion and the chapter's task: the vocabulary behind it.

sections.heading: Where the Marketplace Ends: Four Models
sections.controlling_idea: Listing marketplaces are classified first by endpoint, and the four models (classifieds, lead generation, transactional, managed) form a ladder on which each rung adds what the platform must do, know and carry.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the endpoint axis and the four rungs of the ladder.

transition_in.carries_over: Ingrid's first question, where does our job end.
transition_in.introduces: A precise definition of endpoint and its four values.

flow.rationale: One definition per rung, top to bottom, then the ladder that combines them, then the one model that sits off it; the ladder cannot be read before its rungs are defined.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing marketplace publishes many suppliers' offers, and this book classifies it first by endpoint: the last step of the transaction the platform takes responsibility for.
Classifieds are marketplaces whose job ends when a buyer contacts a seller; payment and handover happen off the platform.

evidence.what: Meta, 2016: 'Facebook does not facilitate the payment or delivery of items in Marketplace'.
evidence.shows: States the classifieds endpoint in one documented sentence.

transition_in.introduces: Its first value: the contact.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the platform never sees the money, classifieds monetize visibility and access, and even a group with a declared transactional push earns most of its revenue that way.

evidence.what: Adevinta 2023: classifieds €1,399M of €1,826M revenue, advertising €312M, transactional €103M (about 77%, 17%, 6%).
evidence.shows: Visibility and access remain the main revenue years into a transactional push.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform does not take part in the sale.
transition_in.introduces: What it can therefore charge for.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A lead-generation marketplace ends when a qualified enquiry reaches a professional, so it must qualify, count, route and attribute leads and prove their value at renewal.

transition_in.carries_over: Classifieds, which end at the contact.
transition_in.introduces: The next rung, which delivers a lead to someone who pays for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Documented lead-generation models differ in how professionals pay and who receives the lead.

evidence.what: Rightmove ARPA £1,621/month (2025); Autotrader ARPR £2,995/month (FY26); Zillow share of voice and pay-at-close (10-K 2025); AVIV France commission share (2023); Homes.com 'your-listing your lead' (CoStar 10-K 2025).
evidence.shows: Pricing on value delivered takes several documented forms, each needing different lead data.

transition_in.carries_over: The lead as the unit of value.
transition_in.introduces: The ways professionals pay for it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Pay-at-close pricing pulls the portal into the transaction's outcome without its money, which makes outcome matching a reconciliation problem rather than a payments problem.

transition_in.introduces: What it demands of the systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A transactional marketplace ends when payment and delivery are complete on the platform, and its revenue becomes a take rate on GMV that classifieds cannot observe.

evidence.what: eBay take rate 13.94% on GMV of $79.6B (2025); a16z (2020) GMV versus revenue; Gurley (2012) 'if you bring the cash, you are king'.
evidence.shows: Defines take rate and GMV from documented sources and shows why being in the payment flow attracts groups.

transition_in.introduces: The rung where the money passes through the platform.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vinted is the clearest example of a marketplace built transactional from the start, with integrated shipping and payment and a buyer fee as its main charge.

evidence.what: Vinted 2025: GMV €10.8B, revenue €1.1B; buyer fee 'usually 5% + $0.70' in the US (price list 2026).
evidence.shows: Shows a transactional model at scale and where its revenue comes from.

transition_in.introduces: Its clearest documented case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A managed marketplace takes inventory, quality or outcome risk itself, by buying and reselling, guaranteeing results or curating like a retailer.

evidence.what: Autotrader's Autorama: about 1,350 vehicles temporarily on balance sheet (FY26); iBuying in real estate.
evidence.shows: Shows the managed rung exists inside classifieds groups.

transition_in.introduces: One step further: the platform carries the risk.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four models form a ladder on which each rung adds what the platform must do, know and carry.

evidence.what: The endpoint ladder table: endpoint, what the platform observes, monetization, who holds money and risk, documented examples.
evidence.shows: Puts the four definitions side by side so the added load per rung is visible.

evidence.what: Figure 1: descending steps with a heavier load on each.
evidence.shows: Shows the cumulative load.

transition_in.introduces: Their order as a ladder.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Software for professionals is an adjacent model off the ladder, whose customer is the professional and whose architecture follows SaaS rules.

evidence.what: Scout24 Transaction Enablement €106.6M (2025); Zillow's Follow Up Boss.
evidence.shows: Shows such businesses sit inside marketplace groups.

transition_in.introduces: A business that is in the group but not on the ladder.

sections.heading: Six Axes, One Profile
sections.controlling_idea: The endpoint is one of six independent axes that together form a marketplace profile for one country and category, and a brand usually holds several profiles.

advances_thesis.how: Adds the other five axes and makes the profile, not the brand, the unit.

transition_in.carries_over: The endpoint, the most consequential axis.
transition_in.introduces: The other five axes and the profile they form.

flow.rationale: The profile first, then each axis in the table's order, then the consequence for brands; the conclusion needs every axis before it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six axes vary independently and together form a marketplace profile: the combination of answers that describes one marketplace in one country and category; Ingrid's five questions covered five of them, and scope is the sixth.

evidence.what: Axis table: endpoint, scope, seller type, item identity, money flow, risk ownership, with values and what each decides first.
evidence.shows: Gives each axis its values and the system decision it drives first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Horizontal marketplaces cover many categories with mostly private supply and vertical ones specialize in a high-value domain with professional supply, and their economics differ sharply.

evidence.what: Rightmove and Autotrader operating margins of about 70%; Adevinta's French margin falling two points with a growing transactional share (2023).
evidence.shows: Scope and seller mix change margins; the paragraph says the two figures are not like for like (Adevinta's drop comes from adding transaction services) and that margins follow the mix of scope, seller type and endpoint.

transition_in.introduces: The scope axis, named as the second axis in the table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Horizontal groups also contain verticals, and the same unbundling inside a group can set a horizontal brand's car section against a sister vertical brand.

evidence.what: Parker (2010) on the spawn of craigslist; Adevinta's 2023 reorganization by vertical; OLX motors, real estate and jobs at 71% of revenue (FY26).
evidence.shows: Verticals are carved out of horizontals both by startups and inside groups.

transition_in.introduces: That the line runs inside groups too, which is Veldmark's Polish problem.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seller type matters because consumers and professionals respond to different prices and the trader line decides which consumer-protection rules apply.

transition_in.introduces: The seller-type axis.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Item identity decides how much of a listing can be derived rather than typed.

evidence.what: Unique second-hand goods; vehicles with a VIN; properties with an address and parcel; catalog products.
evidence.shows: Shows four levels of identity and what each lets the platform derive.

transition_in.introduces: The item-identity axis.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Money flow and risk ownership are separate questions: a platform can route money without holding it, and carry buyer-protection losses without owning inventory.

evidence.what: eBay books losses 'resulting from our buyer protection programs, chargebacks' as transaction losses (10-K 2025).
evidence.shows: Buyer protection is a liability to provision, not only a fee.

transition_in.introduces: The last two axes and why they are kept apart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A brand is not a profile: Tradeyard alone holds ten, so a platform that encodes the profile by brand is wrong somewhere and needs code changes whenever a category moves.

transition_in.introduces: What follows for how the profile is stored.

sections.heading: Vertical Differences
sections.controlling_idea: The endpoint and the other axes take typical values in each vertical, each with its own taxonomy trap.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the axes by vertical, so the reader can place a vertical on the ladder and name the trap it invites.

transition_in.carries_over: The six axes and the profile they form.
transition_in.introduces: The typical profile, and the classification trap, of each vertical.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Profiles cluster by vertical: each vertical has a typical endpoint, supply, item identity, money flow and monetization unit, which places it on the ladder, and a typical classification trap.

evidence.what: Vertical table: general classifieds, real estate, automotive, jobs, recommerce.
evidence.shows: Sorts the verticals onto the ladder (goods at contact or payment; property, cars and jobs at a lead or application; recommerce at delivery) and names the trap each invites.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two cells of the vertical table have already become product rules at documented companies: Indeed's performance billing (the jobs row's monetization unit) and Vinted's separate professional channel (the recommerce row's supply column, the seller-type axis); the endpoint axis reaches further still, which leads into the next section.

evidence.what: Indeed bills on 'clicks or started applications' (n.d.); Vinted Pro separates commercial sellers because 'businesses have legal obligations that private sellers don't' (2026).
evidence.shows: Axes become product and software boundaries.

transition_in.introduces: Two documented products in which single cells of the table (the jobs monetization unit, the recommerce supply split) became product rules.

flow.rationale: The whole vertical table first, then two documented products that show single axes enforced; the products need the table's columns to be read as axes.

sections.heading: What Each Model Asks of the Architecture
sections.controlling_idea: Each step down the ladder changes nearly every system, most surprisingly what the platform can observe, which identity and regulatory obligations apply, and who holds the money.

advances_thesis.how: Maps each rung to its contexts, data, identity, trust and regulatory consequences.

transition_in.carries_over: The axes and their typical values per vertical.
transition_in.introduces: The axis that reaches furthest into the systems: what each endpoint value demands of them.

flow.rationale: The whole consequence table first, then the pipeline view, then the three consequences that most surprise architects, each from the table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Of the six axes defined earlier, the endpoint reaches furthest: moving down the endpoint ladder changes nearly every system, not just one.

evidence.what: Consequences table: identity depth, core new contexts, trust focus, ranking signal, monetization system, data kept, regulatory switch, per model.
evidence.shows: Shows each rung's demands across seven concerns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every rung adds contexts and none replaces the ones before it, so a category that moves its endpoint must run the extra contexts for that category alone.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the endpoint ladder as a pipeline.
evidence.shows: Shows inheritance of contexts from left to right.

transition_in.introduces: The same consequences seen as a pipeline.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A classifieds platform does not know whether a sale happened; it sees contacts, while lead portals sometimes see outcomes and transactional marketplaces see the order.

evidence.what: OLX Tech (2022): learning-to-rank labels were purchases or 'messages/calls to sellers' 'because transactions aren't always confirmed'.
evidence.shows: A documented ranking system had to use contacts as the success label.

transition_in.introduces: The least obvious one: observability of outcomes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What the platform can observe decides what ranking optimizes, what experiments measure and what can be sold.

evidence.what: Zillow treats pay-at-close fees as variable consideration and estimates lead-to-transaction conversion (10-K 2025).
evidence.shows: Pricing on outcomes the platform cannot see requires an attribution pipeline.

transition_in.introduces: What that limits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each rung down switches on more identity and regulatory obligations, such as EU trader traceability and ranking disclosure, because both rules attach to what the platform lets consumers do, not to what it lists.

evidence.what: DSA Article 30 (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065); Omnibus Directive (EU) 2019/2161 definition of online marketplace and ranking parameters.
evidence.shows: Regulation attaches to what the platform enables, so it deepens with the endpoint.

transition_in.introduces: Identity and regulation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adding payments switches on seller tax reporting under DAC7 that a pure classifieds site may not have, a reading to confirm with counsel.

evidence.what: Belastingdienst DAC7 guidance (n.d.); commentary that listing-only platforms fall outside.
evidence.shows: Shows a reporting obligation that follows knowledge of payments.

transition_in.introduces: The obligation payments switch on.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Classifieds groups that add payments almost always keep the money with a licensed payment service provider and own the flow around it.

evidence.what: Kleinanzeigen 'Sicher bezahlen' holds funds up to 14 days (n.d.); Marktplaats withdrew Gelijk Oversteken in April 2022 and runs Kopersbescherming through OPP with a 5% buyer fee (2022).
evidence.shows: The provider owns the regulated money; the marketplace owns offer, fees, labels, timer and disputes.

transition_in.introduces: How groups hold the money itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The step beyond is a licence of one's own, which brings safeguarding, a ledger that reconciles to the cent and supervisory reporting.

evidence.what: Vinted Pay EMI licence from the Bank of Lithuania; own wallet from January 2026.
evidence.shows: A marketplace can move from partner to licensed entity, taking on the obligations.

transition_in.introduces: Money held by the marketplace's own licensed entity.

sections.heading: In Practice: Moving Along the Ladder
sections.controlling_idea: Documented marketplaces moved along the ladder in both directions: horizontals added payments only for goods, some transactional and managed pushes were scaled back, and lead portals moved closer to the deal.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the documented record that the endpoint moves both ways and category by category.

transition_in.carries_over: What each rung adds to the systems.
transition_in.introduces: What happened when real marketplaces took that on or gave it up by changing rungs.

flow.rationale: Four patterns, from the most common advance to retreats, then the middle path; each pattern is a group of documented cases followed by what they show.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The documented history shows movement along the ladder in both directions, in four recurring patterns.
The large European horizontals added payments and shipping for shippable goods while keeping classifieds for everything else.

evidence.what: leboncoin transactional since 2019, revenue €53M (2022) to €73M (2023); Marktplaats transactional 2017, shipping 2019, second carrier 2022; Kleinanzeigen's 2023 ambition (Adevinta reports 2019, 2023).
evidence.shows: Three horizontals moved goods toward the transaction.

transition_in.introduces: Pattern 1.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: None of them moved cars or homes, so the transactional layer was category-gated to shippable, moderately priced goods.

evidence.what: mobile.de earned essentially no transactional revenue in 2023.
evidence.shows: Even inside the same group the vertical stayed off the transactional rung.

transition_in.introduces: What they did not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The transactional layer also cost margin, so it may be right but is not a free revenue line.

evidence.what: Transactional revenue 5.6% of Adevinta's 2023 revenue; French margin diluted; rising direct payment and shipping costs.
evidence.shows: The move carries direct costs.

transition_in.introduces: The cost of the layer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Some groups pushed transactions further and then pulled back.

evidence.what: OLX Pay&Ship (OLX Tech 2023) de-prioritized in Europe (Prosus FY25); Adevinta's 2023 unified platform followed by a 2025 decentralized model (strategic report 2025).
evidence.shows: Transactional pushes are reversible decisions.

transition_in.introduces: Pattern 2: pushes scaled back.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The most expensive moves were down to the managed rung, and all three documented cases retreated.

evidence.what: Zillow Offers wound down 2 November 2021 with a $304.4M write-down; OLX Autos $1.6B revenue then $206M half-year losses and exit announced March 2023; CarGurus wound down CarOffer on 6 August 2025.
evidence.shows: Managed models retreated when prices turned.

transition_in.introduces: Pattern 3: retreats from the managed rung.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The managed rung changes what a model error costs: an estimate that informs a listing page becomes a balance-sheet loss when the platform buys at it.

evidence.what: A 7% valuation error under adverse selection.
evidence.shows: Explains why classifieds groups' systems and capital fit the rungs above.

transition_in.introduces: Their common thread.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vertical portals move closer to the deal without holding money or assets, and professionals can push back when the new step changes their workflow.

evidence.what: Autotrader Deal Builder enquiries 'convert at double the rate' and a 1.7% forecourt drop partly attributed to its roll-out (FY26); mobile.de lead API (2026).
evidence.shows: The lead endpoint extends toward reservations, with commercial risk.

transition_in.introduces: Pattern 4: lead generation moves closer to the deal.

sections.heading: Veldmark: Four Brands, Twenty Profiles
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark records its twenty profiles in a reviewed register, which sizes the shared checkout by the profiles that need it rather than by brand.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the profile and the both-directions lesson to one group, showing what is shared beneath the endpoint and what is not.

transition_in.carries_over: The documented moves, category by category and in both directions.
transition_in.introduces: What Veldmark does with that lesson: a register of profiles.

flow.rationale: The register as a whole, what it implies for the shared platform, its hardest row resolved, then two instances; resolving Poland straight after the register closes the thread the scene opened before the examples move to single listings.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ingrid's grid became the marketplace profile register, a short versioned table reviewed whenever a brand proposes to change its model.

evidence.what: Register summary: brand rows with profile counts, endpoint, seller type, money flow, risk carried, monetization (2026).

sections.heading: Trade-offs: Where Should the Marketplace End?
sections.controlling_idea: Each endpoint option has a place where it is right and wrong, and two judgements follow: treat every move down as a bet with an exit plan, and keep the endpoint in data, not code.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the ladder and the record into the chapter's two recommendations.

transition_in.carries_over: Veldmark's register and the documented moves.
transition_in.introduces: The question every leadership team returns to: should we move the endpoint?

flow.rationale: The options table first, then the two judgements it supports, the second following from the first: a cheap exit needs the endpoint in data.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every leadership team returns to whether to move the endpoint, and each option has its gains, costs and conditions.

evidence.what: Trade-off table: stop at contact, own the lead, own the transaction, own the outcome, hybrid category-gated; gains, costs, when right, when wrong.
evidence.shows: Lets a reader pick the option that fits a category.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: I would treat every move down the ladder as a bet with an exit plan whose architecture makes the retreat cheap.

evidence.shows: Contrasts a cheap and an expensive reversal.

sections.heading: Failure Modes
sections.controlling_idea: The taxonomy fails in seven recognizable ways, each traceable to a model that was assumed, hidden or mismeasured.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what goes wrong when the endpoint is not recorded per profile and its consequences are not designed.

transition_in.introduces: How it fails in practice.

flow.rationale: The most common and costly failure first, ending with the one that concerns the model off the ladder.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The taxonomy fails in practice in seven recognizable ways.
Assuming one model for the whole group fits transactional goods and hurts every other brand, which is how The Forced Fit begins.

transition_in.introduces: The most common.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When the endpoint is never written down it is hidden in code, and changing a category means finding every place that assumes it.

transition_in.introduces: A model never written down.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A transactional pivot launched as a feature ships the screen before the ledger, disputes and reporting.

transition_in.introduces: A pivot launched as a feature.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ignoring contact-stage fraud because the platform does not handle money is Fast Mail for Fraudsters, because messaging is where money is negotiated.

evidence.what: At 20:11 on Sunday 7 March 2027 a fake Safe Deal payment link reached Femke from a domain registered that day.
evidence.shows: Fraud concentrates at the endpoint, even impersonating the platform's own payment brand.

transition_in.introduces: A failure at the contact endpoint.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Revenue from different rungs is not comparable, and reporting it in one field makes portfolio decisions harder.

evidence.what: OLX Autos briefly made up just over half of OLX's classifieds revenue while losing money.
evidence.shows: Principal revenue can swamp subscription revenue in reports.

transition_in.introduces: Revenue across rungs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Borrowing the success event from the wrong model optimizes the wrong thing, which is Vanity Liquidity: counting what is easy to count instead of what the model delivers.

transition_in.introduces: Success mismeasured.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Software for professionals that publishes to rivals creates a neutrality obligation, which at Veldmark is a taxonomy decision as much as a governance one.

evidence.what: Veldmark's March 2027 decision: no Keybridge agency data used by Hearthly for ranking or sales targeting, with access controls and an annual independent review.
evidence.shows: Registering Keybridge as SaaS rather than supply decides its obligations.

transition_in.introduces: The off-ladder model's failure.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: At group scale the taxonomy is four standing decisions: a profile register as an architecture artifact, separate decision rights, sharing beneath the endpoint first, and design for movement both ways, plus four things to watch.

advances_thesis.how: States how a group keeps the endpoint recorded, governed and reversible.

transition_in.introduces: The standing decisions that prevent them.

flow.rationale: Announce the four decisions, give them in the order record, decide, share, reverse, then what to watch once they are in place.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The seven failures share a remedy: at group scale the taxonomy is a set of standing decisions, of which four matter most.
Make the profile register an architecture artifact, written per country and category and reviewed when it changes.

evidence.what: Veldmark's twenty-row register, versioned like a decision record.
evidence.shows: Shows the artifact at the size of one page.

transition_in.introduces: The first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Moving an endpoint is a commercial decision, but architecture owns the cost of change and must be consulted early.

transition_in.introduces: Who decides changes to it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Share the capabilities every profile needs first, and share rung-specific contexts only among the profiles that use them.

evidence.what: Adevinta's 2019 rule to centralize where 'investment requirements are large and the technology is uniform', and its 2023–2025 swing.
evidence.shows: The rule works per capability, not per brand.

transition_in.introduces: What to share.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Design for movement in both directions so a retreat is a configuration change and a retention plan, not a migration.

transition_in.introduces: How to keep moves reversible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Whether the four decisions hold shows in four signals at group level: the mix of contacts, leads and orders per profile, the success event, the regulatory switches and the cost per profile, all of which should change with the endpoint; if they do not, the register and the shared platforms have not followed the move.

transition_in.introduces: The signals that show whether they hold.

evidence.shows: Each question maps to a section of the chapter.

conclusion.heading: From Model to Liquidity
conclusion.synthesis: The five answers from the opening were each right for some rows of the register; recorded per country and category, they stop being a disagreement about the business and become configuration the systems read, with every move along the ladder a category-gated bet with an exit plan.
conclusion.so_what: A group that records its profiles can size shared platforms by the profiles that need them and change a category's endpoint without a program, instead of building one brand's model into everyone's systems.

callback.to: The five people's five answers in the opening paragraph.
callback.how: Each answer is shown to be the endpoint of particular rows in the register.

takeaway.content: Write the profile register for your own group, then measure whether each profile's job is being done well.

hand_off.introduces: What all of them sell underneath, liquidity, and how to measure whether the job is being done well.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The five answers from the opening were each right for some rows of the register, so recording the model per country and category turns a disagreement about the business into configuration the systems can read, and makes each move along the ladder a category-gated bet that can be reversed.
